passages.t: Zion, wake and dress for a festival
passages.happening:
“Awake, awake, clothe yourself with strength, O Zion!” (verse 1). Jerusalem is to put on her garments of splendor, for the unclean will no longer enter her (verse 1). She is to shake off her dust, rise and sit on her throne, and take the chains from her neck (verse 2).

‘You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed’ (verse 3). God reviews the history. His people went down to Egypt to live, and Assyria oppressed them without cause (verse 4). Now they have been taken away again for nothing, their rulers taunt them, and God's name is blasphemed all day long (verse 5).

‘Therefore My people will know My name’ (verse 6). On that day they will know that he is the one who speaks.
passages.hearers:
The double call to wake rang out in 51:9 to the arm of the LORD and in 51:17 to Jerusalem drunk with the cup. Here it comes a third time, to Zion herself, and now she is told to dress for a festival. Everything since chapter 40 has been building to this: God is coming home to Jerusalem and bringing his people with him.

Verses 3 to 5 compress Israel's history into three stages of oppression: Egypt, then Assyria, which destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC and devastated Judah in 701 BC, and now Babylon, unnamed here, which deported Judeans and burned the temple. Clay tablets published in 2014, many from a Babylonian settlement called Al-Yahudu, Judahtown, dated from 572 BC onward, show Judean exiles living as tenant farmers on crown land.

The language comes from family law. A go'el, a kinsman-redeemer, bought back a relative sold into debt, as Boaz did for Naomi's family. God received no price when he handed his people over, so he owes no price to take them back. They were sold for nothing; they will be redeemed for nothing.
passages.later: Boaz acted as the kinsman-redeemer for Naomi's family in Ruth 4. And Revelation says of the new Jerusalem what verse 1 says of Zion: ‘nothing unclean will ever enter it’ (Revelation 21:27).
passages.hard:
Verse 1 promises that the unclean will no longer enter Jerusalem. Did that promise fail?

The objection is plain. The return under Cyrus was small and struggling, and Jerusalem was entered and defiled again: by Antiochus IV, who set up a pagan altar in the temple in 167 BC, by Pompey in 63 BC, and by the Romans, who destroyed the temple in AD 70. Skeptical readers see this as a prophecy that history did not meet.

Those who read the promise as God's word answer in more than one way. Many Jewish interpreters read the chapter as a promise of final redemption still awaited. Many Christian interpreters read it in stages: a first fulfillment in the return from Babylon, a deeper one in the coming of the Servant, and a final one in the new Jerusalem, where nothing unclean will enter. Both traditions read it as a promise whose last word has not yet been spoken.
passages.asks: Zion is told to shake off her dust and take the chains from her own neck. Ask what chains God has already broken that you are still wearing. And ask what it would look like to dress for the festival before you can see it.

passages.t: Beautiful feet on the mountains: your God reigns
passages.happening:
‘How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation’ (verse 7). The messengers say to Zion that her God reigns (verse 7).

The watchmen lift their voices and shout for joy, ‘For every eye will see when the LORD returns to Zion’ (verse 8). ‘Break forth in joy, sing together, O ruins of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem’ (verse 9). ‘The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations’ (verse 10), and all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of God.

Then the fourth double command. “Depart, depart, go out from there! Touch no unclean thing” (verse 11), you who carry the vessels of the LORD. They will not leave in haste, as at the exodus, ‘for the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
News in the ancient world travelled on foot. Watchmen on a city's walls could see a runner coming over the hills long before he arrived, and they tried to read his news from the way he ran. Here the runner brings the best news possible: peace, good, salvation, and the words Your God reigns. To a people whose God had seemed beaten by Babylon's gods, it was the announcement that he was king after all. It echoes the cry of the temple psalms, The LORD reigns.

The word for bringing good news is basar. When Jewish translators put the Hebrew Bible into Greek, they used the word from which the New Testament's word for preaching the gospel comes.

The vessels of verse 11 are the gold and silver articles Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple. Ezra records that Cyrus gave them back, and that Sheshbazzar brought 5,400 of them from Babylon to Jerusalem. At the exodus Israel left in haste. This time God walks in front and behind.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 7 for the apostles who are sent: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” (Romans 10:15). Nahum uses almost the same words for the herald of Nineveh's fall, and Paul takes up verse 11: ‘Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you’ (2 Corinthians 6:17).
passages.asks: The herald's whole message is that God reigns. Ask what would change in your week if that were the first news you heard each morning. And ask what it means to you that God goes both before you and behind you.

passages.t: The Servant exalted, and marred beyond human likeness
passages.happening:
Then, with no warning, the Servant appears again. ‘Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted’ (verse 13).

Many were appalled at him. His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and his form marred beyond human likeness (verse 14). ‘So He will sprinkle many nations. Kings will shut their mouths because of Him’ (verse 15). ‘For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
These three verses open the fourth and last Servant Song, which runs to the end of chapter 53. The placement matters. The good news that God reigns comes first, and then the portrait of a disfigured Servant, as if the two belong together.

The song begins at the end. Before it tells of the Servant's suffering, it tells of his exaltation. The word translated prosper also means to act wisely. However his path looked at the time, it will prove to have been the wise one.

Verse 15 has a question of translation. The BSB reads sprinkle, the word priests used for sprinkling blood or water in rites of cleansing. If that is the word, the Servant does for many nations what a priest did for Israel. The grammar is unusual, though, and the old Greek translation reads that many nations will marvel at him. Many scholars take it from another root meaning to startle. English Bibles divide on it.

Kings, who were used to speaking, fall silent before what they had never been told.
passages.later: Paul reads verse 15 as the reason he preaches where Christ is not yet named: “Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand” (Romans 15:21). The same song continues in Isaiah 53, which Acts 8 and 1 Peter 2 read as fulfilled in Jesus.
passages.asks: The song starts with the Servant lifted up and only then tells of his suffering. Ask how knowing the end of a story changes how you read the hard middle of it. And ask what you have heard about the Servant that you were never told before.
